content: Hemidesmus indicus, commonly known as Indian Sarsaparilla, is a plant species native to South Asia. It is characterized as a slender, laticiferous, twining shrub that can sometimes grow in a prostrate or semi-erect form. The roots of this plant are woody and possess a distinct aromatic quality. Its stems are numerous, slender, cylindrical, and exhibit thickened nodes. The leaves are arranged oppositely, are short-petioled, and display significant variability in shape, ranging from elliptic-oblong to linear-lanceolate forms. The flowers are greenish on the exterior and purplish on the interior, and they are densely clustered in sub-sessile axillary cymes. This plant is utilized in the preparation of beverages and holds a significant place in traditional medicine. In Ayurvedic medicine, it is referred to as Ananthamoola or Anantmula and is also known as False Sarsaparilla. Hemidesmus indicus is recognized for its therapeutic properties, functioning as a tonic, alterative, demulcent, diaphoretic, diuretic, and blood purifier. It is employed in the treatment of various conditions, including nutritional disorders, syphilis, chronic rheumatism, urinary diseases such as gravel, and skin conditions. The plant is administered in different forms, such as powder, infusion, or decoction, often prepared as a syrup. Additionally, it is a component of several medicinal formulations. In Ayurvedic practice, Hemidesmus indicus is classified as a Rasayana plant, indicating its anabolic effects. It stimulates bile flow and aids in the detoxification of the body. The plant is an effective diuretic, capable of increasing urine output by three to four times. When combined with Tinospora, its therapeutic effects are further enhanced. It is particularly beneficial in alleviating inflammation of the urethra, relieving burning sensations during urination, and addressing advanced stages of syphilis (third or fourth stages). However, it is sometimes confused with another Ayurvedic herb known as White Sariva or Smilax ovalifolia. Chemical analysis of the root of Hemidesmus indicus has revealed the presence of coumarins, volatile oils (with p-methoxy salicylic aldehyde as the chief component), two sterols, and a pregnane glycoside. The plant is widely distributed across India, from the upper Gangetic plain extending eastward to Assam, as well as in certain regions of central, western, and southern India.
